observations.text: SP recalled the critical action procedures at the level expected for this training unit, with the IP naming the condition and directing the sequence of the BOLD FACE steps. Two of the four procedures requested in the pre-flight briefing were stated by heart once started, but no procedure was initiated from the Check List flow alone. Marginal performance for the Training Section - independent recall of the emergency procedures set as daily assignment is expected to develop over the following sorties.

SP, applying the BOLD FACE steps studied as daily assignment, stated the critical action procedure for the simulated malfunction after verbal prompts from the IP on the first two steps, and no part of the procedure had to be executed by the IP. The step taken out of the standardized sequence was recognized and corrected with a short delay, and the follow-on Check List items were then completed. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP stated the BOLD FACE steps by heart with two minor errors of wording, each recognized and corrected in a timely manner without IP's intervention. The follow-on Check List and IFG items for the simulated emergency were completed in the standardized sequence, and the A/C limits of Section V applicable to the condition were quoted correctly. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP stated all critical action procedures requested in the pre-flight briefing by heart, in sequence and without mistakes, and executed the simulated emergency in flight according to the Check List and the IFG without IP's intervention. The emergency was handled effectively, with aircraft control maintained throughout the procedure. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP stated every BOLD FACE procedure requested by heart, in sequence and without a single mistake, and related each step to the affected system as set in the daily assignment. During the sortie the simulated emergency was handled effectively from the first indication to the completion of the IFG items, with the applicable Section V limits observed and stated aloud. Accuracy and speed in the emergency procedures were above the level expected at this stage of training. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP, due to memorization of the BOLD FACE steps as isolated items rather than as a sequence, could not state the critical action procedure for the simulated malfunction without assistance, stopping after the second step. The result was that the IP had to direct the remaining steps and execute part of the follow-on Check List items. Further study of the emergency procedures and of the relevant systems set as daily assignment is required.

SP, due to a startle response that displaced the memorized recovery sequence, did not initiate the BOLD FACE steps for the unannounced simulated malfunction, and the aircraft state was left unmonitored during the first seconds. The IP had to direct the procedure and execute part of it before the Check List was resumed. Recognition of the condition and of the critical action procedure that applies to it requires further study.

SP completed the emergency procedure at the level required for this training unit, stating the BOLD FACE steps after verbal prompts from the IP at the first and the third step. The two steps taken out of the standardized sequence were recognized and corrected with delay, and no part of the procedure had to be executed by the IP. Marginal performance for the Training Section - recall of the critical action procedures by heart, without prompting, is expected to improve in the following sorties.

SP stated the BOLD FACE steps by heart with two minor errors in the order of the follow-on Check List items, each recognized and corrected in a timely manner without IP's intervention. The simulated emergency was handled effectively and the A/C limits of Section V applicable to the condition were observed throughout. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP stated all critical action procedures by heart, in sequence and without mistakes, and executed the simulated emergency according to the Check List and the IFG without IP's intervention. Execution was timely and standardized, and the affected system was identified from its indications before the first action was taken. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP stated every BOLD FACE procedure requested, by heart and without mistakes, and explained the behavior of the affected systems as set in the daily assignment. The simulated emergency in flight was handled effectively and flawlessly, with the IFG items completed in the standardized sequence and the Section V limits observed at each stage. Speed and accuracy in the emergency procedures exceeded the standard for this training unit. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP, due to an incomplete study of the critical action procedures set as daily assignment, could not state the BOLD FACE steps for the simulated emergency without assistance, omitting three of the required steps in the pre-flight briefing. The IP had to direct the sequence and execute part of the Check List items during the subsequent practice in flight. Further study of the emergency procedures and of the relevant systems is required.

SP, due to locking onto one malfunction instead of continuing to fly the aircraft, did not begin the BOLD FACE steps for the presented condition and left the aircraft state unmonitored. The IP had to take the A/C and direct the critical action procedure from the first step. The emergency was not handled effectively, and the priority of flying the A/C before working the procedure requires further study.

SP, due to recall of the BOLD FACE steps by their wording rather than by their sequence in the Check List, stated the critical action procedure for the simulated emergency only after verbal prompts from the IP at two steps. The transposed step was recognized and corrected with delay, and the IFG items were then completed without IP's intervention. Recall of the critical action procedures by heart requires further study.

SP, due to insufficient knowledge of the affected system and of its indications, did not associate the presented condition with the corresponding BOLD FACE procedure and started the steps of an adjacent procedure instead. The error was corrected only after the IP's verbal prompt, with the result that the emergency was handled with delay. Detailed knowledge of the emergency procedures and of the relevant systems, set as daily assignment, requires further study.

SP executed the emergency procedure within the desired standards, stating the BOLD FACE steps by heart and completing the Check List items without IP's intervention. Two steps were transposed in the standardized sequence and were recognized and corrected in a timely manner, and the pace of the procedure was slower than the standard for this unit. Marginal performance for the Training Section - speed in the execution of the critical action procedures is expected to improve while the present accuracy is maintained.

SP stated all critical action procedures by heart, in sequence and without mistakes, and executed the simulated emergency according to the Check List and the IFG without IP's intervention. Execution was timely and standardized, and the A/C limits of Section V were observed throughout the recovery. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP stated every BOLD FACE procedure requested in the briefing, by heart and without mistakes, and identified the affected system from its indications before any action was taken. The simulated emergency was handled effectively and flawlessly, the IFG items were completed in the standardized sequence, and the A/C was kept within the Section V limits at every stage. Accuracy and speed in the emergency procedures were above the level expected for this training unit. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP, due to a Check List flow rehearsed only in the briefing room and never applied in the cockpit, could not complete the emergency procedure without assistance when the malfunction was introduced during the working phase, leaving three IFG items unaddressed. The IP had to take the A/C and execute part of the procedure. Further study of the emergency procedures and practice of their execution in flight are required.

SP, due to absent explicit role assignment when the malfunction occurred, did not state who was flying the A/C and who was working the procedure, and the BOLD FACE steps were left unstarted while both cockpits worked the indication. The IP had to assume control and direct the critical action procedure. The emergency was not handled effectively, and the transfer of aircraft control during abnormal conditions requires further study.

SP, due to reading the Check List items without cross-referring them to the expanded procedure of the IFG, completed the emergency procedure only after verbal prompts from the IP on two of the follow-on items. The omission was recognized and corrected with delay, after the A/C had already been configured for the recovery. Execution of the emergency procedures in the standardized sequence requires further practice.

SP, due to an unmanaged stress response after the abnormal indication, stated the BOLD FACE steps out of the prescribed sequence and did not complete them by heart, requiring the IP's verbal prompts on the last two steps. The transposed steps were recognized with delay, although no part of the procedure had to be executed by the IP. Composure and pacing at the onset of an emergency are expected to improve with further practice.

SP, due to a rushed first pass through the Check List, omitted one follow-on item of the emergency procedure after the BOLD FACE steps had been stated correctly. The omission was recognized and corrected in a timely manner without IP's intervention, and the remaining items were executed in the standardized sequence. The error was minor and the emergency was handled effectively, within the A/C limits of Section V.

SP, due to failure to monitor the aircraft state after the configuration change required by the procedure, allowed the airspeed to decay below the glide speed briefed for the simulated emergency while working the IFG items. The deviation was minor and was recognized and corrected in a timely manner without IP's intervention, and the BOLD FACE steps had been stated by heart and in sequence. Handling of the emergency remained effective and within the limits of Section V.

SP executed the emergency procedures within the desired standards, stating the BOLD FACE steps by heart and in sequence and completing the Check List and IFG items without IP's intervention. The first action after the malfunction was taken later than the standard for this unit, and one step was re-checked before the sequence continued. Marginal performance for the Training Section - timeliness in initiating the critical action procedures is expected to improve while the present accuracy is maintained.

SP stated every BOLD FACE procedure by heart, in sequence and without mistakes, both in the pre-flight briefing and when required in flight, and identified the affected system from its indications before the first action. The emergency was handled effectively and flawlessly, with the Check List and IFG items completed in the standardized sequence and without IP's intervention, and the A/C limits of Section V were observed throughout. Knowledge of the relevant systems set as daily assignment was demonstrated in detail during the post-flight briefing. Above end of block MIF achieved.
